# Hacker Courses: every course

> 1,376 online courses recommended in 3,371 public Hacker News comments, 2006 to October 2026, in rank order. CC BY 4.0: cite https://hackercourses.com/ and link the course page.

## #1 Machine Learning (Andrew Ng) (Coursera)

Page: https://hackercourses.com/course/machine-learning-andrew-ng/
Course website: https://www.coursera.org/learn/machine-learning
Topic: Machine Learning & AI; Level: beginner; Cost: free; Format: video lectures
Recommended by 240 people in 226 threads, 2009–2026. Badges: Classic, Evergreen.
Tags: machine learning, neural networks, octave, andrew ng, introductory

Andrew Ng's introductory machine learning course on Coursera, covering supervised and unsupervised learning, linear and logistic regression, neural networks, and practical advice on applying ML. It originated as the Stanford 'ML Class' in 2011 and uses Octave for programming assignments.
Why people recommend it: Commenters call it a great introduction that avoids heavy math while still conveying real understanding of the topic, and many say it was their starting point.

## #2 6.001 Structure and Interpretation of Computer Programs (MIT OpenCourseWare)

Page: https://hackercourses.com/course/6-001-structure-and-interpretation-of-computer-programs/
Course website: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/electrical-engineering-and-computer-science/6-001-structure-and-interpretation-of-computer-programs-spring-2005/
Topic: Programming Languages; Level: intermediate; Cost: free; Format: video lectures
Recommended by 88 people in 96 threads, 2007–2026. Badges: Classic, Evergreen.
Tags: sicp, scheme, lisp, abelson, sussman, recursion, interpreters

MIT's introductory course on Structure and Interpretation of Computer Programs, built around the SICP textbook and Abelson and Sussman lectures, teaching abstraction, recursion, interpreters and functional-style program design mostly through Scheme/Lisp. Lecture videos and materials are freely available through MIT OpenCourseWare.
Why people recommend it: Commenters repeatedly describe it as eye-opening and foundational, calling the lectures and book a must-study for anyone wanting to think more deeply about programming.

## #3 The Elements of Computing Systems (Nand2Tetris) (nand2tetris.org)

Page: https://hackercourses.com/course/the-elements-of-computing-systems-nand2tetris/
Course website: https://www.nand2tetris.org/
Topic: CS Fundamentals & Systems; Level: intermediate; Cost: free; Format: project-based
Recommended by 87 people in 83 threads, 2010–2026. Badges: Classic, Evergreen.
Tags: computer architecture, assembler, compilers, operating systems, nand gates, schocken

The Elements of Computing Systems (Nand2Tetris) is a project-based course in which you build a working computer from NAND gates upward: logic gates, a CPU, memory, an assembler, a virtual machine, a high-level language compiler, and a simple operating system, ending with a game.
Why people recommend it: Commenters call it a fantastic, practical way to understand how computers work from first principles, with one saying it is probably the best course they have taken.

## #4 Practical Deep Learning for Coders (fast.ai)

Page: https://hackercourses.com/course/practical-deep-learning-for-coders/
Course website: https://course.fast.ai/
Topic: Machine Learning & AI; Level: beginner; Cost: free; Format: video lectures
Recommended by 112 people in 101 threads, 2017–2026. Badges: Classic, Evergreen.
Tags: deep learning, pytorch, practical, howard, transfer learning

A free, top-down, hands-on deep learning course by Jeremy Howard and Rachel Thomas at fast.ai that teaches practitioners to build working models with PyTorch and Jupyter notebooks, with relatively little emphasis on theory. A companion Part 2 covers more advanced topics such as diffusion models.
Why people recommend it: Commenters repeatedly call it the best practical entry point into deep learning for programmers, praising its focus on building working models quickly without requiring a heavy math background.

## #5 18.06 Linear Algebra (Gilbert Strang) (MIT OpenCourseWare)

Page: https://hackercourses.com/course/18-06-linear-algebra-gilbert-strang/
Course website: http://ocw.mit.edu/courses/mathematics/18-06-linear-algebra-spring-2010/
Topic: Mathematics; Level: beginner; Cost: free; Format: video lectures
Recommended by 78 people in 76 threads, 2009–2026. Badges: Classic, Evergreen.
Tags: linear algebra, matrices, eigenvalues, svd, strang, mit ocw

MIT's undergraduate introductory linear algebra course taught by Gilbert Strang, covering matrices, vector spaces, eigenvalues, and the singular value decomposition, with video lectures, syllabus, and problem sets published through MIT OpenCourseWare.
Why people recommend it: Commenters call it the best linear algebra resource available, praising Strang's intuitive, unassuming lecturing style and how it clarifies concepts like the SVD and the four fundamental subspaces.

## #6 CS50: Introduction to Computer Science (Harvard University)

Page: https://hackercourses.com/course/cs50-introduction-to-computer-science/
Course website: https://cs50.harvard.edu
Topic: CS Fundamentals & Systems; Level: beginner; Cost: free; Format: video lectures
Recommended by 72 people in 73 threads, 2012–2026. Badges: Classic, Evergreen.
Tags: introduction to computer science, c, python, algorithms, malan

CS50 is Harvard's introductory computer science course, covering programming fundamentals in C, Python, and web technologies along with algorithms, data structures, and problem-solving. It is offered free through Harvard's public course site and edX.
Why people recommend it: Commenters repeatedly call it an excellent, high-production-value intro that builds a strong foundation, with David Malan's lecturing singled out as a major strength.

## #7 Learning How to Learn: Powerful mental tools to help you master tough subjects (Coursera)

Page: https://hackercourses.com/course/learning-how-to-learn-powerful-mental-tools-to-help-you-master-tough-s/
Course website: https://www.coursera.org/learn/learning-how-to-learn
Topic: General Learning; Level: beginner; Cost: free; Format: video lectures
Recommended by 60 people in 69 threads, 2014–2025. Badges: Classic, Evergreen.
Tags: learning techniques, memory, procrastination, metacognition, oakley

A short Coursera course by Barbara Oakley (with Terrence Sejnowski) on the cognitive science of learning, covering topics such as chunking, memory, procrastination, and focused versus diffused modes of thinking. It is aimed at improving how people study rather than teaching a specific subject.
Why people recommend it: Commenters call it a fundamental, quick course that improves study habits and helps with procrastination and retention, and often recommend it before other learning.

## #8 Cryptography I (Coursera)

Page: https://hackercourses.com/course/cryptography-i/
Course website: https://www.coursera.org/learn/crypto
Topic: Security & Cryptography; Level: intermediate; Cost: free; Format: video lectures
Recommended by 41 people in 47 threads, 2012–2025. Badges: Classic, Evergreen.
Tags: cryptography, block ciphers, attacks, math, boneh

An introductory Coursera course by Dan Boneh (Stanford) covering the fundamentals and math of cryptography, including practical exercises such as breaking flawed constructions. It is the first of a two-part sequence, with Cryptography II as the follow-up.
Why people recommend it: Commenters repeatedly call it one of the best courses they have taken, praising its clear, thorough explanations of crypto fundamentals and its hands-on attack exercises.

## #9 Functional Programming Principles in Scala (Coursera)

Page: https://hackercourses.com/course/functional-programming-principles-in-scala/
Course website: https://www.coursera.org/course/progfun
Topic: Programming Languages; Level: beginner; Cost: freemium; Format: interactive MOOC
Recommended by 42 people in 41 threads, 2012–2026. Badges: Classic, Evergreen.
Tags: scala, functional programming, odersky, recursion, coursera

Martin Odersky's introductory MOOC on functional programming using Scala, covering recursion, higher-order functions, immutable data, pattern matching, and collections. It is based largely on SICP-style exercises and includes automatically graded programming assignments.
Why people recommend it: Commenters call it an excellent, well-taught introduction to functional programming, praising Odersky as a lecturer and the course's automated grader and assignments.

## #10 CS193P Developing Applications for iOS using SwiftUI (Stanford University)

Page: https://hackercourses.com/course/cs193p-developing-applications-for-ios-using-swiftui/
Course website: http://www.stanford.edu/class/cs193p/cgi-bin/index.php
Topic: Web & Mobile Development; Level: beginner; Cost: free; Format: video lectures
Recommended by 39 people in 40 threads, 2009–2025. Badges: Classic, Evergreen.
Tags: ios, swift, swiftui, objective-c, hegarty, stanford

CS193P is Stanford's iOS application development course, taught by Paul Hegarty, with free lecture videos and assignments covering Objective-C, Cocoa Touch, and later SwiftUI. Commenters describe it as a structured, lecture-based introduction to building iPhone apps.
Why people recommend it: Commenters repeatedly call the Stanford iOS lectures excellent and free, saying they give a structured, conceptual foundation that tutorials and sample code do not.

## #11 Algorithms, Part I (Coursera)

Page: https://hackercourses.com/course/algorithms-part-i/
Course website: https://www.coursera.org/learn/algorithms-part1
Topic: Algorithms & Data Structures; Level: beginner; Cost: free; Format: interactive MOOC
Recommended by 38 people in 41 threads, 2012–2025. Badges: Classic, Evergreen.
Tags: algorithms, data structures, java, union-find, sedgewick

Algorithms, Part I is Robert Sedgewick's introductory Princeton course on Coursera, covering fundamental data structures and algorithms such as union-find, stacks, queues, sorting, and searching, with Java programming assignments. It is the first of a two-part sequence.
Why people recommend it: Commenters call it an engaging, well-organized free introduction to algorithms and data structures, with visualizations and assignments that teach practical implementation and interview-relevant skills.

## #12 CS61A: Structure and Interpretation of Computer Programs (UC Berkeley)

Page: https://hackercourses.com/course/cs61a-structure-and-interpretation-of-computer-programs/
Course website: http://inst.eecs.berkeley.edu/classes-eecs.html
Topic: Algorithms & Data Structures; Level: beginner; Cost: free; Format: video lectures
Recommended by 31 people in 31 threads, 2008–2026. Badges: Classic, Evergreen.
Tags: sicp, scheme, python, recursion, harvey

CS 61A is UC Berkeley's introductory computer science course built around the textbook Structure and Interpretation of Computer Programs (SICP), covering programming abstraction, recursion, interpreters, and related topics, historically taught in Scheme and later in Python. Commenters also point to its self-paced Scheme-based variant (CS 61AS) and to lecture archives from Brian Harvey.
Why people recommend it: Commenters call it the best introductory CS course and praise its SICP-based approach and Brian Harvey's lectures.

## #13 CS231n: Convolutional Neural Networks for Visual Recognition (Stanford University)

Page: https://hackercourses.com/course/cs231n-convolutional-neural-networks-for-visual-recognition/
Course website: http://cs231n.stanford.edu/index.html
Topic: Machine Learning & AI; Level: intermediate; Cost: free; Format: mixed
Recommended by 39 people in 41 threads, 2015–2024. Badges: Classic, Evergreen.
Tags: convolutional neural networks, deep learning, computer vision, backpropagation, karpathy, stanford

Stanford's CS231n covers convolutional neural networks and deep learning for visual recognition, including backpropagation, training networks, CNNs, and related architectures, with course notes, assignments, and lectures. It is taught with a hands-on, assignment-driven approach.
Why people recommend it: Commenters repeatedly call it an excellent, hands-on introduction to deep learning and neural networks, praising the course notes, assignments, and Karpathy's teaching.

## #14 6.006 Introduction to Algorithms (MIT OpenCourseWare)

Page: https://hackercourses.com/course/6-006-introduction-to-algorithms/
Course website: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/electrical-engineering-and-computer-science/6-006-introduction-to-algorithms-fall-2011/
Topic: Algorithms & Data Structures; Level: intermediate; Cost: free; Format: video lectures
Recommended by 27 people in 29 threads, 2009–2024. Badges: Classic, Evergreen.
Tags: algorithms, data structures, complexity, clrs, mit ocw

MIT's undergraduate introduction to algorithms and data structures, covering asymptotic analysis, sorting, hashing, graph search, and dynamic programming, with lecture videos and materials on MIT OpenCourseWare. It follows the CLRS textbook.
Why people recommend it: Commenters call it a good intro to data structures and algorithms that helped with complexity intuition and technical interviews, and say it pairs well with CLRS.

## #15 Programming Languages (Dan Grossman) (Coursera)

Page: https://hackercourses.com/course/programming-languages-dan-grossman/
Course website: https://www.coursera.org/learn/programming-languages
Topic: Programming Languages; Level: intermediate; Cost: free; Format: video lectures
Recommended by 30 people in 33 threads, 2013–2023. Badges: Classic, Evergreen.
Tags: programming languages, functional programming, standard ml, racket, ruby, grossman

A Coursera course by Dan Grossman (University of Washington) that teaches programming language fundamentals through Standard ML, Racket, and Ruby, covering functional programming, recursion, types, pattern matching, and language design trade-offs. Commenters describe it as a three-part sequence.
Why people recommend it: Commenters call it an excellent, well-structured introduction to programming language concepts and functional programming, and several say it changed how they approach learning new languages.

## #16 Deep Learning Specialization (Andrew Ng) (Coursera)

Page: https://hackercourses.com/course/deep-learning-specialization-andrew-ng/
Course website: https://www.coursera.org/specializations/deep-learning
Topic: Machine Learning & AI; Level: intermediate; Cost: paid; Format: interactive MOOC
Recommended by 31 people in 31 threads, 2017–2025. Badges: Classic, Evergreen.
Tags: deep learning, neural networks, coursera, andrew ng, backpropagation, sequence models

A five-course Coursera specialization by Andrew Ng, offered through deeplearning.ai, covering neural networks, hyperparameter tuning and project structure, convolutional networks, and sequence models. It builds from the math of neural networks up to applied deep learning.
Why people recommend it: Commenters call it excellent and phenomenal, praise its theory-first approach that builds understanding of what happens under the hood, and say the assignments help clarify concepts.

## #17 Introduction to Computer Science and Programming in Python (MIT OpenCourseWare)

Page: https://hackercourses.com/course/introduction-to-computer-science-and-programming-in-python/

MIT's introductory computer science course taught in Python, covering core programming and computational problem-solving with lecture videos, problem sets, and the course textbook. It is offered free through MIT OpenCourseWare and was also run on edX as MITx 6.00.
Why people recommend it: Commenters repeatedly call it a very good, free introduction to CS and programming that teaches concepts transferable to any language, and several say it was the course that gave them real programming ability.

## #18 Human Behavioral Biology (Robert Sapolsky) (Stanford University)

Robert Sapolsky's Stanford course on human behavioral biology, taught as a lecture series that explains behavior across levels from genes and brain chemistry to evolution and culture. The lectures are freely available on YouTube.
Why people recommend it: Commenters call it accessible, engaging, and deep, and several say it changed how they think about behavior, aggression, and depression.

## #19 Neural Networks for Machine Learning (Geoffrey Hinton) (Coursera)

Page: https://hackercourses.com/course/neural-networks-for-machine-learning-geoffrey-hinton/
Course website: https://www.coursera.org/learn/neural-networks
Topic: Machine Learning & AI; Level: advanced; Cost: free; Format: video lectures
Recommended by 25 people in 32 threads, 2012–2025. Badges: Classic, Evergreen.
Tags: neural networks, backpropagation, deep learning, hinton, machine learning

Geoffrey Hinton's Coursera course on neural networks for machine learning, covering feedforward and recurrent networks, backpropagation, and deep learning fundamentals from one of the field's pioneers. It is a graduate-level course with a theoretical lean and demanding exercises.
Why people recommend it: Commenters call it an excellent, challenging introduction to neural networks taught by a pioneer, and several say it changed the course of their careers.

## #20 CS229 Machine Learning (Stanford University)

Page: https://hackercourses.com/course/cs229-machine-learning/
Course website: http://cs229.stanford.edu/
Topic: Machine Learning & AI; Level: advanced; Cost: free; Format: video lectures
Recommended by 20 people in 24 threads, 2007–2023. Badges: Classic, Evergreen.
Tags: andrew ng, machine learning, statistics, linear algebra, supervised learning

Stanford's graduate-level machine learning course taught by Andrew Ng, covering the theory and math behind common learning algorithms, with lecture videos and course notes available online. It assumes a strong background in probability and linear algebra.
Why people recommend it: Commenters call it one of the best ML courses out there, praised for deriving algorithms from the math and for its clear, rigorous treatment compared with the lighter Coursera version.

## #21 Learning From Data (Caltech)

Page: https://hackercourses.com/course/learning-from-data/
Course website: https://www.edx.org/course/learning-from-data-introductory-machine-learning
Topic: Machine Learning & AI; Level: intermediate; Cost: free; Format: video lectures
Recommended by 20 people in 23 threads, 2012–2025. Badges: Classic, Evergreen.
Tags: machine learning, learning theory, vc dimension, regularization, abu-mostafa

Yaser Abu-Mostafa's Caltech course on the theoretical foundations of machine learning, covering generalization, VC dimension, regularization, validation, and linear and nonlinear models. Available as free video lectures on the instructor's site and, at times, on edX, with an accompanying book.
Why people recommend it: Commenters call it an outstanding, rigorous introduction to the theory behind machine learning, more mathematical than Andrew Ng's Coursera class and taught with exceptional clarity.

## #22 15-445/645 Intro to Database Systems (Carnegie Mellon University)

Page: https://hackercourses.com/course/15-445-645-intro-to-database-systems/

Topic: Databases & Data Engineering; Level: intermediate; Cost: free; Format: video lectures
Recommended by 17 people in 20 threads, 2017–2025. Badges: Classic, Evergreen.
Tags: database internals, sql, indexing, concurrency control, pavlo

CMU's introductory database systems course covering how DBMSs are designed and built: data models, storage, indexing, concurrency control, recovery, and query processing. Lectures are published free on YouTube, and homework is available on the course site.
Why people recommend it: Commenters repeatedly call it top-notch and praise Andy Pavlo's clear, free video lectures on how databases work internally.

## #23 Introduction to Databases (Stanford University)

An introductory Stanford course by Jennifer Widom covering relational databases, relational theory and algebra, and SQL, with lectures and problem sets. It has run as a Stanford MOOC in several sessions, with self-paced versions on Lagunita.
Why people recommend it: Commenters call it one of the best MOOCs they've taken, praising its well-planned exercises and its blend of database theory with real-world examples.

## #24 6.824 Distributed Systems (MIT OpenCourseWare)

Page: https://hackercourses.com/course/6-824-distributed-systems/
Course website: https://courses.engr.illinois.edu/cs425/
Topic: CS Fundamentals & Systems; Level: advanced; Cost: free; Format: mixed
Recommended by 16 people in 15 threads, 2013–2025. Badges: Classic, Evergreen.
Tags: distributed systems, raft, consensus, mapreduce, golang, robert morris

MIT's graduate-level distributed systems course, with published lecture notes, assigned readings of classic papers, and Go labs that build pieces such as MapReduce, Raft consensus, and a sharded key-value store. Lectures and materials are openly available on MIT OpenCourseWare and YouTube.
Why people recommend it: Commenters call it an excellent, hands-on introduction to distributed systems, valuable because the labs force you to implement and debug real designs.

## #25 Algorithms: Design and Analysis, Part 1 (Coursera)

Stanford's introductory algorithms course taught by Tim Roughgarden covering asymptotic analysis, divide and conquer, sorting, and graph algorithms, with programming assignments checked against data sets. It was offered on Coursera and later moved to edX.
Why people recommend it: Commenters call it a challenging, well-taught course with practical implementation assignments that work in any language, and recommend it for interview prep and for learning algorithms.

Harvard's introductory probability course taught by Joe Blitzstein, covering probability basics and problem solving, with video lectures, problem sets, and a companion textbook. Lectures and materials are freely available online and it is also offered on edX.

## #27 CS188 Introduction to Artificial Intelligence (UC Berkeley)

CS188 is UC Berkeley's introductory artificial intelligence course, covering classical AI such as search, game playing, and probabilistic reasoning, with later material on machine learning. Its assignments are built around the Pacman projects, and an edX version offered the first half of the material.

## #28 The Theoretical Minimum (Leonard Susskind) (YouTube)

A Stanford continuing-education lecture series by physicist Leonard Susskind, with companion books, covering classical mechanics, quantum mechanics, special and general relativity, and related topics at roughly upper-high-school to lower-undergraduate math level. Commenters point to free YouTube playlists and the theoreticalminimum.com course page.

## #29 Probabilistic Graphical Models (Coursera)

An advanced Coursera course by Daphne Koller on probabilistic graphical models, covering Bayesian networks, Markov networks, inference, and learning. It is based on the Koller and Friedman textbook and is noted for demanding homework.

## #30 15-213 Introduction to Computer Systems (Carnegie Mellon University)

Carnegie Mellon's undergraduate introduction to computer systems, covering how programs run at the level of machine code, memory, linking, and the operating system, built around labs such as the bomb lab and malloc lab. ## #31 6.042J Mathematics for Computer Science (MIT OpenCourseWare)

MIT's undergraduate discrete mathematics course covering logic, proof techniques, sets, number theory, graph theory, probability and related tools used in computer science. ## #33 Model Thinking (Coursera)

Page: https://hackercourses.com/course/model-thinking/
Course website: https://www.coursera.org/learn/model-thinking
Topic: General Learning; Level: beginner; Cost: free; Format: video lectures
Recommended by 12 people in 12 threads, 2014–2023. Badges: Evergreen.
Tags: mental models, systems thinking, simulation, segregation model, page

Model Thinking is a Coursera course by Scott E. Page that introduces a range of formal and informal models, such as segregation, tipping points, and network and collective-behavior models, for reasoning about the world. It is offered free to audit, with paid certificates available.
Why people recommend it: Commenters call it insanely useful, the best course on Coursera, and a great introduction to thinking in models, often recommending it as a free course.

## #34 Neural Networks: Zero to Hero (YouTube)

Page: https://hackercourses.com/course/neural-networks-zero-to-hero/
Course website: https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLAqhIrjkxbuWI23v9cThsA9GvCAUhRvKZ
Topic: Machine Learning & AI; Level: beginner; Cost: free; Format: video lectures
Recommended by 16 people in 16 threads, 2022–2025.
Tags: neural networks, backpropagation, transformers, gpt, karpathy

A series of YouTube video lectures by Andrej Karpathy that builds neural networks from the ground up, starting with a small autograd and backpropagation engine and working up to a simplified GPT-style language model. Lectures are followed along in a Jupyter notebook.
Why people recommend it: Commenters call it a clear, hands-on way to understand backpropagation and transformers, with Karpathy's explanations of attention singled out as especially accessible.

## #35 15-721 Advanced Database Systems (Carnegie Mellon University)

Page: https://hackercourses.com/course/15-721-advanced-database-systems/
Course website: https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLSE8ODhjZXjagqlf1NxuBQwaMkrHXi-iz
Topic: Databases & Data Engineering; Level: advanced; Cost: free; Format: video lectures
Recommended by 12 people in 15 threads, 2017–2023.
Tags: database internals, concurrency control, query execution, in-memory databases, pavlo
